analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to offer reasonable accommodations to pregnant workers, like lighter duty or schedule changes, unless doing so is an undue hardship.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 10 senators behind it in September 2012, the bill never got a hearing or a vote and died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it illegal for employers to refuse reasonable accommodations to workers whose ability to do their job is limited by pregnancy, childbirth, or related medical conditions, as long as the accommodation does not create an undue hardship for the business. It also barred employers from forcing a pregnant worker onto unpaid leave when an accommodation could work instead, and from penalizing applicants because they might need an accommodation. Enforcement would run through the same procedures used for sex discrimination claims under the Civil Rights Act.
analysis.who_benefits: Pregnant workers and job applicants, especially those in physically demanding or inflexible jobs who currently face a choice between working in unsafe conditions and taking unpaid leave they may not be able to afford. Under the bill, employers would have to provide accommodations such as modified duties, schedule changes, or extra breaks, and workers could sue or file charges if they were refused, denied opportunities, or retaliated against.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Pregnant workers, especially in physical jobs

how_it_helps.text: Makes it an unlawful employment practice to refuse a reasonable accommodation for known limits related to pregnancy, childbirth, or related medical conditions, unless the employer shows undue hardship.
Bars employers from forcing a pregnant employee to take leave when another reasonable accommodation could be provided instead.
Bars employers from denying job opportunities based on the need to accommodate, and from requiring a worker to accept an accommodation she did not ask for.
Lets workers enforce these rights through the same powers, procedures, and remedies used under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, including damages, attorney's fees, and a prohibition on retaliation.

analysis.who_pays: Employers covered by civil rights employment law generally, plus employment agencies and labor organizations, bear the cost of providing accommodations (modified duties, schedule flexibility, equipment) and the risk of discrimination claims and damages when they do not.

drawbacks.text: Covered employers bear the cost of accommodations and new exposure to lawsuits and damages; the bill adopts the Americans with Disabilities Act's undue-hardship standard but still shifts compliance and litigation costs onto businesses.
Protections would not take effect immediately: the EEOC would have up to two years after enactment to issue regulations identifying what accommodations must be provided.
The accommodation duty is defined by regulation and by how courts have construed the ADA, leaving room for disputes over what counts as reasonable and who qualifies.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete for a specific group: pregnant workers who today must often choose between unsafe working conditions and unpaid leave would get a legal right to modest adjustments, with an undue-hardship escape valve for employers. The costs are real but bounded, and the same framework has operated for decades under the disability-accommodation law this bill borrows from. The main weakness is timing and enforcement detail rather than design.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in late September 2012, read twice, and referred to the Senate committee that handles labor bills, where it sat with no hearing, no vote, and no further action until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Robert Casey introduced the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act in the Senate on September 19, 2012, joined by original cosponsors including Senators Shaheen, Lautenberg, Harkin, and Mikulski.
On the day it was introduced, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
That referral was the last action of any kind: the bill received no committee markup, no floor vote, and no further consideration before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.
Support was limited to the sponsor and nine cosponsors, eight Democrats and one Independent; no Republican senators sponsored or cosponsored the bill in the record.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers are better off: no new accommodation duty, compliance costs, or litigation exposure took effect during this Congress. Pregnant workers gained nothing; the protections the bill would have created never became law in this session.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor in the record was a Democrat or Independent and no Republican signed on, but the bill never reached a vote, so actual partisan opposition was never measured.

industries.industry: Employers (businesses covered by Title VII, generally 15 or more employees)
industries.note: The bill would have required them to accommodate pregnancy-related limitations or prove undue hardship, adding compliance costs and exposure to damages claims. The cost to them is the protection working pregnant women would have gained.
The ban on refusing pregnancy accommodations applies to them as well as to employers, so they faced the same compliance and liability exposure.
